semin-durr:25-25.t:
His saying: {فَاقِرَةٌ}: it is the great calamity; it was so named because it breaks the vertebrae (faqār) of the back. al-Nābigha said:
4418 - أَبَى لِيَ قَبْرٌ لا يزالُ مُقابِليْ ... وضَرْبَةُ فَأْسٍ فوقَ رَأْسيَ فاقِرَهْ
(A grave that ever faces me, and the blow of an axe upon my head, a back-breaking one, refused me [rest].)
That is: a calamity that leaves its mark. From this the poor man (al-faqīr) was named, because his vertebrae are broken by want; this has already been discussed in al-Baqara.

semin-durr:26-26.t:
His saying: {التراقي}: the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of «بَلَغَتْ», and the fāʿil (agent) is an implied pronoun [referring] to the soul, even though it has not been mentioned, as in the saying of Ḥātim:
4419 - أماوِيَّ ما يُغْنِي الثَّراءُ عن الفتى ... إذا حَشْرَجَتْ يوماً وضاقَ بها الصدرُ
(O Māwiyya, wealth avails a man nothing when one day it rattles [in his throat] and the chest is straitened by it.)
That is: when the soul rattles. It has been said about the verse: what points to the soul is the mention of the whole that comprises it, namely the wealthy man; likewise here the mention of the human being points to the soul. And al-tarāqī is the plural of tarquwa; its origin is tarāqiw, whose wāw was changed into yāʾ because of the kasra before it. The tarquwa is one of the bones of the chest — so said the Shaykh, but what is well known is otherwise. al-Zamakhsharī said: «Every human has two tarquwas»; on this basis it belongs to the pattern of "thick of eyebrows" and "broad of shoulders". al-Tarāqī is the place of the death-rattle. [The poet] said:
4420 - ورُبَّ عظيمةٍ دافَعتُ عنها ... وقد بلغَتْ نفوسُهُمُ التراقِيْ
(And many a grave matter I have warded off from them, when their souls had reached the collarbones.)
al-Rāghib said: «The tarquwa is a bone joining what lies between the hollow of the throat and the shoulder» — end of quote. al-Zamakhsharī said: «The bones flanking the hollow of the throat on the right and the left.» Its pattern is faʿluwa, so the tāʾ is radical and the wāw is augmentative; this is shown by the lexicographers entering it under the root «تَرَق». Abū al-Baqāʾ said: «al-Tarāqī is the plural of tarquwa», and it is faʿluwa, not tafʿula, since there is no «رقو» in the language. «التراقي» has been read with a sukūn on the yāʾ, which is like Zayd's reading «تُطْعِمون أهالِيْكم» [al-Māʾida: 89]; its justification has already been given.

semin-durr:27-27.t:
His saying: {مَنْ رَاقٍ}: a mubtadaʾ (subject) and khabar (predicate). This clause is what stands in the place of the agent [of «قيل»], whereas the principles of the Basrans require that it not be so, since for them the agent cannot be a clause; rather, what stands in its place is the pronoun of the maṣdar (verbal noun). The verification of this was given at the beginning of al-Baqara. This interrogative may be in its proper sense, or it may express deeming unlikely and disapproval. And «راقٍ» is an active participle: either from raqā yarqī, from al-ruqya, which is speech prepared for seeking a cure, with which the sick person is recited over so that he be cured — in the ḥadīth: «And what made you know that it is a ruqya?», meaning al-Fātiḥa, and this is one of its names — or from raqiya yarqā, from al-ruqiyy, which is ascending; that is: the angels, owing to their aversion to his spirit, say: "Who will ascend with this spirit?" One says raqā with fatḥa from al-ruqya, and with kasra from al-ruqiyy. Ḥafṣ paused on the nūn of «مَنْ» with a slight pause (sakta); this was discussed at the beginning of al-Kahf with its verification. Sībawayh mentioned that the nūn is obligatorily assimilated into the rāʾ, with nasalisation (ghunna) and without it, as in: مَنْ راشِدٌ.
What governs «إذا بلغَت» is the meaning of His saying: {إلى رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ المساق}, that is: when it reaches the throat it is raised to Allah, «and His saying:» and it is said: who is a healer «is conjoined to» بَلَغَت «.
[Translator's note: the quotation marks in this last sentence are misplaced in the source text; the intended sense is: "and His saying «وقيل مَنْ راقٍ» is conjoined to «بَلَغَت»".]
And al-masāq is mafʿal from al-sawq (driving), and it is a noun of the maṣdar (ism maṣdar).

semin-durr:31-31.t:
His saying: {فَلاَ صَدَّقَ}: «لا» here has entered upon the past verb, which is widespread in their speech, in the sense of: he did not believe and did not pray. [The poet] said:
4421 - إنْ تَغْفِر اللهمَّ تَغْفِرْ جَمَّا ... وأيُّ عبدٍ لكَ لا ألَمَّا
(If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive abundantly; and which servant of Yours has not committed some small sin?)
Another said:
4422 - وأيُّ خَميسٍ لا أَفَأْنا نِهابَه ... وأسيافُنا مِنْ كَبْشِه تَقْطُر الدِّما
(And which army have we not taken its plunder as spoil, while our swords drip blood from its leader?)
Some also adduced as evidence for this the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
4423 - كأنَّ دِثاراً حَلَّقَتْ بلَبُوْنِه ... عُقابُ تَنُوْفَى لا عُقابُ القواعِلِ
(As if a Tanūfā eagle, not an eagle of the low hills, had soared away with Dithār's milch-camels.)
So his saying «لا عُقابُ» is conjoined to «عُقابُ تَنُوفَى», which is nominative as the agent of «حلَّقَتْ»; [Translator's note: i.e. some took «لا عُقابُ» as «لا» negating a verb «حلَّقت» understood]. The first two verses render this one unnecessary.
Makkī said: «The second "لا" is a negation, not a conjunction, and its meaning is: he did not believe and did not pray.» I say: how could conjunction be imagined so that he needed to deny it? al-Zamakhsharī made {فَلاَ صَدَّقَ وَلاَ صلى} conjoined to the clause in His saying: {يَسْأَلُ أَيَّانَ يَوْمُ القيامة}; he said: «It is conjoined to His saying "يَسْأل أيَّان", i.e. he does not believe in the resurrection, so he did not believe in the Messenger and the Qurʾān», and the Shaykh considered this far-fetched.

semin-durr:32-32.t: His saying: {ولكن كَذَّبَ}: the istidrāk (rectification) here is clear, because the negation of giving in charity [Translator's note: the source writes «التصدُّق» (giving charity) here] and of prayer does not entail denial and turning away, since many Muslims are like that. So He rectified this by [stating] that its cause is denial and turning away. For this reason it is weak to take the negation of «صَدَّقَ» as the negation of believing the Messenger, lest repetition follow, so that «لكنْ» would fall between two concordant [statements], which is not permissible.

semin-durr:33-33.t:
His saying: {يتمطى}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) clause from the agent of «ذَهَبَ»; it may also be in the sense of: he began swaggering, as in [the poet's] saying:
4424 - فقامَ يَذُوْدُ الناسُ عنها. . . . . ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(And he set about driving people away from it …)
Regarding «تمطَّى» there are two views. The first: it is from al-maṭā, and al-maṭā is the back; its meaning is "he swaggers", i.e. he stretches out his back and twists it in swaggering in his gait. The second: its origin is yatamaṭṭaṭu, from tamaṭṭaṭa, i.e. he stretched; its meaning is that he stretches himself in his gait out of swagger, and that is a concomitant of swaggering. So it is close to the meaning of the first but differs from it in its root, since the root of al-maṭā is m-ṭ-w and the root of the second is m-ṭ-ṭ. The third ṭāʾ was only changed into yāʾ out of dislike for bearing identical letters, as in taẓannaytu and qaṣṣaytu aẓfārī ("I clipped my nails"), and [the poet's] saying:
4425 - تَقَضِّيَ البازِيْ إذا البازِيْ كَسرْ
(Like the swooping of the falcon when the falcon folds its wings [to dive].)
And al-muṭayṭāʾ is swaggering and stretching the arms in walking, and al-maṭīṭa is the thick water at the bottom of the basin, because it spreads out, i.e. stretches in it.

semin-durr:34-34.t:
The discussion of His saying {أولى لَكَ فأولى} has preceded in full at the end of Sūrat al-Qitāl; it was only repeated here for emphasis in threat and warning. al-Khansāʾ said:
4426 - هَمَمْتُ بنفسِيَ كلَّ الهمومِ ... فأَوْلَى لنفسِيَ أَوْلَى لها
(I resolved upon my soul every resolve — woe to my soul, woe to it!)
Abū al-Baqāʾ said here: «Regarding the pattern of "أَوْلَى" there are two views. The first: faʿlā, with the alif in it for ilḥāq (assimilation to a pattern), not for the feminine. The second: it is afʿal. On both views it is here [a proper name], and for that reason it does not take tanwīn. What indicates it is what Abū Zayd related in "al-Nawādir": "هي أَوْلاةُ" with the tāʾ, as a diptote. On this basis "أَوْلى" is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and "لك" the khabar (predicate). The second: that it be a verbal noun (ism fiʿl), indeclinable, meaning: evil after evil has come close to you, and "لك" is explanatory (tabyīn).»

semin-durr:36-36.t:
His saying: {سُدًى}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the deputy agent of «يُتْرَكُ», and its meaning is: neglected. One says: ibilun sudā, i.e. neglected camels. The poet said:
4427 - وأُقْسِمُ بالله جَهْدَ اليمينِ ... ما خَلَقَ اللَّهُ شيئاً سُدَى
(And I swear by Allah with the most solemn oath: Allah did not create anything in vain.)
That is: neglected. And asdaytu ḥājatī means: I neglected it. And the meaning of «أَسْدَى إليه معروفاً» (he did him a favour) is: he made it as though it were lost with the one to whom it was done, not mentioning it nor reproaching him with it.
[Translator's note: the source says «حالٌ مِنْ فاعلِ "يُتْرَكُ"»; «يُتْرَكُ» is passive, so its "agent" here means its deputy agent.]

semin-durr:37-37.t:
His saying: {أَلَمْ يَكُ نُطْفَةً}: the generality [of readers] have the yāʾ (from below) in «يك», referring back to the human being. al-Ḥasan [read it] with the tāʾ of address, by way of iltifāt (shift of person) towards him, in rebuke of him.
His saying: {يمنى}: Ḥafṣ read «يُمْنى» with the yāʾ (from below), and there are two aspects to it. The first: the pronoun refers back to al-maniyy (the semen), i.e. it is poured out, so the clause is in the position of a genitive. The second: it refers back to the nuṭfa, because its feminine gender is figurative and because it is in the sense of "water"; Abū al-Baqāʾ said this. But this only holds on the view of Ibn Kaysān; as for the grammarians, they consider it a poetic licence, as in [the poet's] saying:
4428 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... ولا أرضَ أبْقَلَ إبْقالَها
(… nor any land brought forth herbage like its herbage.)
The rest read «تُمْنَى» with the tāʾ (from above), the pronoun being for the nuṭfa. On this reading and on the aspect mentioned just before it, the clause is in the position of an accusative, because it is a naʿt (adjective) of an accusative noun.

semin-durr:39-39.t: His saying: {الذكر والأنثى}: they may be two badals (substitutes) from «الزَّوْجَيْن», or they may be accusative by an implied «أعني» ("I mean") by way of qaṭʿ (cutting off), though the default is its absence. The generality [of readers] read «الزوجَيْن», and Zayd ibn ʿAlī «الزوجان», according to the dialect of those who treat the dual like the maqṣūr noun. Its verification has preceded in Ṭā Hā, together with to whom this dialect is attributed and the evidence for it.

semin-durr:40-40.t:
The generality [of readers] also read «بقادرٍ», an active participle in the genitive by a redundant (zāʾida) bāʾ in the khabar of «ليس». Zayd ibn ʿAlī [read] «يَقْدِرُ», an imperfect verb. The generality [of readers] have «يُحْيِيَ» in the accusative by «أَنْ», because the fatḥa is light on the weak letter. Ṭalḥa ibn Sulaymān and al-Fayyāḍ ibn Ghazwān read it with a sukūn: either he lightened the weak letter by dropping the case vowel, or he treated the connected reading like the pause.
The majority of people hold that undoing the assimilation (idghām) is obligatory. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: «Lest two quiescent letters be combined, actually or virtually.» I say: he means that the ḥāʾ is quiescent, so if we assimilated, we would make the first yāʾ quiescent as well for the assimilation, and two quiescent letters would meet actually, which is impossible to pronounce; so these are two quiescent letters actually. As for his saying «virtually»: some people permitted assimilation in that, reading it «أَنْ يُحِيَّ». That is because, when he wanted to assimilate, he transferred the vowel of the first yāʾ to the ḥāʾ and assimilated it, so two quiescent letters met: the ḥāʾ, because it is virtually quiescent before the transfer to it, and the yāʾ, because its vowel was transferred from it to the ḥāʾ. al-Farrāʾ adduced as evidence for this reading [the poet's] saying:
4429 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... تَمْشِي لسُدَّةِ بيتها فَتُعِيُّ
(… she walks to the threshold of her house and grows weary.)
As for the people of Basra, they do not assimilate it at all; they said: because the vowel of the yāʾ is accidental, since it is for the case ending. Makkī said: «They agreed on non-assimilation in the nominative. As for the accusative, al-Farrāʾ permitted it because the second yāʾ is vowelled, but it is not permissible for the Basrans, because the vowel is accidental.» I say: his claim of consensus is refuted by the verse that I quoted earlier from al-Farrāʾ, namely his saying «فَتُعِيُّ»: this is nominative and it has been assimilated. And that is not far-fetched, because when it was assimilated, that vowel appeared owing to the quiescence of what precedes the yāʾ through the assimilation.

semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying: {لاَ أُقْسِمُ}: The majority read it with the negative «لا». They differed then about it in several analyses. The first: that it negates a preceding statement, as though the disbelievers had said something, and it was said to them "No," and then Allah the Exalted began an oath. The second: that it is redundant. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "They said it is redundant, like it in {لِّئَلاَّ يَعْلَمَ أَهْلُ الكتاب} [al-Ḥadīd: 29] and in his saying:

4402 - في بِئْرِ لاحُورٍ سَرَى وما شَعَرْ
(Gloss: He travelled into a well of «lā ḥūr» and did not perceive it.)

They objected to it that it is made redundant only in the middle of speech, not at its start. They answered that the Quran is in the ruling of a single sūra, its parts connected with one another. The objection is correct, because it occurs as redundant only in the middle of speech, but the answer is not sound. Do you not see how Imruʾ al-Qays made it redundant at the beginning of his ode?" I say: he means his saying:

4403 - لا وأبيك ابنةَ العامرِيْ ... يِ. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Gloss: No, by your father, daughter of the ʿĀmirī ... [rest omitted in the source].)

as will come. This analysis, the objection to it and the answer were transmitted by Makkī and others. The third analysis: Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Introducing the negative «لا» before the verb of oath is widespread in their speech and poetry. Imruʾ al-Qays said:

لا وأبيك ابنةَ العامرِيْ ... يِ لا يَدَّعِي القومُ أنِّي أفِرّْ
(Gloss: No, by your father, daughter of the ʿĀmirī, the people will not claim that I flee.)

And Ghuwayya ibn Sulmī said:

4404 - ألا نادَتْ أُمامةُ باحْتمالِ ... لِتَحْزُنَني فلابِك ما أُبالي
(Gloss: Lo, Umāma called out for departure, to grieve me; [by you] I care not at all.)

Its benefit is to strengthen the oath." Then he said, after relating the analysis of redundancy, the objection and the answer as above: "The proper way is to say: it is for negation, and the meaning in that is that one swears by a thing only to magnify it, as His saying the Exalted indicates to you: {فَلاَ أُقْسِمُ بِمَوَاقِعِ النجوم وَإِنَّهُ لَقَسَمٌ لَّوْ تَعْلَمُونَ عَظِيمٌ} [al-Wāqiʿa: 75-76]. It is as though, by introducing the particle of negation, He says: 'My magnifying it by swearing by it is no magnification at all,' meaning that it deserves more than that. It is also said: «لا» negates a statement that came before that." End of quotation.

His saying "The proper way is to say" up to his saying "it deserves more than that" is a confirmation of his statement "Introducing the negative «لا» before the verb of oath is widespread," to its end. The gist of his speech comes back to its being negative, and the negation bearing on the verb of oath in the sense that he explained; there is no prohibition in it, in wording or meaning. Then he said: "If you ask: His saying {فَلاَ وَرَبِّكَ لاَ يُؤْمِنُونَ} [al-Nisāʾ: 65] and the verses I recited have the thing sworn to negated, so why did you not claim that the «لا» before the oath is added to prepare for the negation after it and to strengthen it, and imply the omitted thing sworn to here as negated, as in your saying «لا أُقْسم بيومِ القيامةِ لا تُتركون سُدى»? I say: if they had restricted the matter to negation without affirmation, there would be room for this view, but it is not restricted. Do you not see how {لاَ أُقْسِمُ بهذا البلد} [al-Balad: 1] is met with His saying {لَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الإنسان}, and likewise His saying {فَلاَ أُقْسِمُ بِمَوَاقِعِ النجوم} [al-Wāqiʿa: 75] with His saying {إِنَّهُ لَقُرْآنٌ كَرِيمٌ}?" This is among the finest points of his speech, so reflect on it. The discussion of this sort has already been given in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ and at the end of al-Wāqiʿa, but here there is an addition to these benefits.

Qunbul and al-Bazzī, with a difference from him, read «لأُقْسِمُ بيوم» with a lām followed by a hamza without an alif. There are four analyses of it. The first: that it is the answer to an implied oath, the implied form being "By Allah, I swear," and the verb is for the present; for that reason the emphatic nūn does not come. This is the view of the Kufans. The Basrans do not allow a present-tense verb to fall as the answer to an oath; if something appears to be that, the verb is made the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, so the answer becomes a nominal clause, with one of its two parts implied; this, for some of them, is of that kind, the implied form being "By Allah, I swear" (with «لأنا أُقْسِمُ»). The second: that it is a future verb, and the emphatic nūn was not brought because the acts of Allah are true and certain, so they need no emphasis, unlike the acts of others. Sībawayh related the omission of the nūn, though it is rare, and the Kufans allow it without rarity, since it is part of their view that the lām and the nūn may take turns. Of the omission of the lām is the poet's saying:

4405 - وقتيلِ مَرَّةَ أَثْأَرَنَّ فإنَّه ... فَرْغٌ وإنَّ أخاكم لم يُثْأَرِ
(Gloss: And the slain of Murra I will avenge, for his blood is unavenged, whereas your brother was not avenged.)

that is, «لأَثْأَرَنَّ». And of the omission of the nūn, which is like the verse, is his saying:

4406 - لَئِنْ تَكُ قد ضاقَتْ عليكم بيوتُكُمْ ... لَيَعْلَمُ ربي أنَّ بيتيَ واسعٌ
(Gloss: If your houses have grown narrow for you, my Lord knows that my house is wide.)

The third: that it is the lām of commencement (lām al-ibtidāʾ), not the lām of oath. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "like {وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَيَحْكُمُ} [al-Naḥl: 124]." But what is known is that the lām of commencement does not enter the imperfect except in the khabar of «إنَّ», like {وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَيَحْكُمُ}. This verse is like the verse in Yūnus [verse 16] {وَلاَ أَدْرَاكُمْ بِهِ}, for the two read it with a short alif, and the discussion on it has already been given. There is no disagreement that «ولا أُقْسِم» has an alif after «لا», because it is written only so, unlike the first, which is written without an alif after «لا»; likewise in His saying {لاَ أُقْسِمُ بهذا البلد} there is no disagreement that it has an alif after «لا».

The answer of the oath is omitted, its implied form being «لتُبْعَثُنَّ» (you will surely be resurrected), indicated by His saying «أيحسَبُ الإِنسانُ». It is also said the answer is «أَيَحْسَبُ». It is also said it is «بلى قادِرين», and this is related from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. It is also said the meaning is the negation of the oath, that is: "I do not swear on anything, but I ask you: does man think...?" These views are anomalous and rejected, and are not sound from those who held them, because they depart from the tongue of the Arabs; I mentioned them only to point out their weakness, as is my custom.

semin-durr:3-3.t: His saying: {أَلَّن}: This is the lightened «أنْ», and its ruling is known from what was said in al-Māʾida and elsewhere. «لن» and what is within its scope are in the position of the khabar, and the separator here is the negative particle. It and what is in its scope fill the place of the two objects of «حَسِبَ», or its one object, according to the disagreement. The majority read «نجمعُ» with the nūn of magnification, with «عظامَه» accusative as direct object. Qatāda read «تُجْمع» with a tāʾ from above with ḍamma, passive, with «عظامُه» nominative as it stands in for the agent.

semin-durr:4-4.t: His saying: {بلى}: It is an affirmation of what comes after the negation over which the interrogative extends. The majority read «قادِرين» in the accusative, and there are two views. The better known: that it is accusative as ḥāl from the agent of the implied verb indicated by the particle of answer, that is, "Yes, We shall gather them, being able." The second: that it is accusative as the khabar of an implied «كان», that is, "Yes, We were able at the beginning," and this is not clear. Ibn Abī ʿAbla and Ibn al-Samayfaʿ read «قادرون» in the nominative, as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "Yes, We are able."

semin-durr:5-5.t:
His saying: {بَلْ يُرِيدُ}: There are two analyses. The first: that «بل» is merely for the transitional leaving-off (iḍrāb intiqālī), without conjunction: He turned away from the first speech and took up another. The second: that it is a conjunction. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "«بل يريد» is conjoined to «أَيَحْسَبُ», so it may, like it, be interrogative, or an affirmation, in that He turns away from one thing asked about to another, or turns away from a question to an affirmation." The Shaykh said, after relating this from al-Zamakhsharī: "These three implied forms are forced and not evident." I say: There are only two implied forms here.

The object of «يريد» is omitted, indicated by the reason in His saying «ليَفْجُرَ أمامَه»; the implied form is: "he wants his desires and his sins, in order to go on in them always and forever." «أمامَه» is accusative as an adverbial, its original being a place, and it is borrowed here for time. The pronoun in «أمامَه» evidently refers to man. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "It refers to the Day of Resurrection, in the sense that he wants his desires so as to be wicked in his denial of the resurrection, before the Day of Resurrection."

semin-durr:6-6.t: His saying: {يَسْأَلُ}: This is a resumptive clause. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "an explanation of «لِيَفْجُرَ»." So it may be resumptive and explanatory, or a badal from the clause before it, because explanation may be by resumption or by badal; but the second is prevented by the nominative form of the verb, for if it were a badal it would be accusative. It may be said that he substituted a clause for a clause, not the particular verb for the verb alone. There is discussion in this; a parallel was given in al-Dhāriyāt and elsewhere.

semin-durr:7-7.t:
His saying: {بَرِقَ}: Nāfiʿ read «بَرَقَ» with fatḥa on the rāʾ, and the rest with kasra. It is said they are two dialects for bewilderment and dazzlement. It is also said: «بَرِقَ» with kasra means he was bewildered in fear. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Its origin is from «بَرِقَ الرجلُ» when he looked at lightning and his sight was dazzled." Others said: as one says «أَسِدَ» and «بَقِرَ» when he sees many lions and cattle and is bewildered by that. Dhū al-Rumma said:

4407 - ولو أنَّ لُقْمانَ الحكيمَ تَعَرَّضَتْ ... لعينَيْهِ مَيٌّ سافِراً كاد يَبْرِقُ
(Gloss: Had Mayy appeared unveiled before the eyes of Luqmān the Wise, he would almost have been dazzled.)

And al-Aʿshā said:

4408 - وكنتُ أَرَى في وجهِ مَيَّةَ لَمْحَةً ... فأَبْرَقُ مغشِيَّاً عليَّ مكانيا
(Gloss: I used to see a gleam in Mayya's face, and I would be dazzled, fainting on the spot.)

And al-Farrāʾ recited:

4409 - فنَفْسَك فانْعَ ولا تَنْعَني ... وداوِ الكُلومَ ولا تَبْرَقِ
(Gloss: Mourn your own soul and do not mourn me; tend the wounds and do not be dazzled.)

«بَرَق» with fatḥa is from «البريق», that is, it gleamed from the intensity of its staring. Abū al-Sammāl read «بَلَقَ» with lām. The lexicographers, except al-Farrāʾ, said its meaning is "opened". One says «بَلَقْتُ البابَ» and «أَبْلَقْتُه», that is, I opened it and parted it. Al-Farrāʾ said: "in the sense of «أَغْلَقْتُه» (I closed it)." Thaʿlab said: "Al-Farrāʾ erred in that." Then it is possible that «بَلَقَ» is a root distinct from «بَرَقَ», and possible that it is one root in which one letter was exchanged for another; the exchange of lām for rāʾ has occurred in several words; they said «نَثَرَ كِنانته» and «نَثَلَها», and they said «وَجِلَ» and «وَجِرَ», so this may be of that kind. It is supported by the fact that «بَرَقَ» has come in the sense of widening and opening his eyes, as Abū ʿUbayda said, and he recited:

4410 - لَمَّا أتاني مِنْ عُمَيْرٍ راغباً ... أَعْطَيْتُه عِيساً صِهاباً فبرَقْ
(Gloss: When ʿUmayr came to me seeking, I gave him reddish-white camels, and he stared wide-eyed.)

that is, he opened his eyes, and this fits «بَلَقَ» in meaning.

semin-durr:8-8.t: His saying: {وَخَسَفَ}: The majority read it in the active voice. Abū Ḥaywa, Ibn Abī ʿAbla and Yazīd ibn Quṭayb read «خُسِفَ» in the passive; this is because «خَسَفَ» is used both intransitively and transitively: one says «خَسَفَ القمرُ» and «خَسَفه الله». It is well known that «الخُسوف» is for the moon and «الكُسوف» for the sun. Some said, rather, both occur with both: one says «خَسَفَتِ الشمسُ» and «كَسَفَتْ», and «خَسَفَ القمرُ» and «كَسَفَ». Some were supported by the hadith: "The sun and the moon are two signs of the signs of Allah; they are not eclipsed (yukhsafān) for the death of anyone," where «الخُسُوف» is used for both. In my view there is something to consider in this, because of the possibility of predominance (taghlīb). And are they of one meaning or not? Abū ʿUbayd and a group said they have one meaning. Ibn Abī Uways said: "«الخُسوف» is the going of all their light, and «الكُسوف» is the going of part of it."

semin-durr:9-9.t:
His saying: {وَجُمِعَ الشمس والقمر}: No sign of the feminine is attached, because the feminine is figurative. It is also said: because masculine predominates. There is something to consider in this: if you said «قام هندٌ وزيدٌ», it would not be permitted according to the majority of the Arabs. Al-Kisāʾī said: "It is carried on the sense: the two luminaries (al-nayyirān) were gathered." «يقولُ الإِنسانُ» is the answer to «إذا» from His saying {فَإِذَا بَرِقَ البصر}. «أينَ المفرُّ» is accusative in position by the saying, and «المَفَرُّ» is a maṣdar in the sense of «الفِرار» (fleeing). This is the well-known reading.

Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, the sons of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan ibn Zayd, among others, read it with fatḥa on the mīm and kasra on the fāʾ; it is the noun of place of fleeing, that is, "where is the place of flight?" Al-Zamakhsharī allowed it to be a maṣdar, saying: "like «المَرْجِعِ»." Al-Ḥasan read the reverse of this, that is, with kasra on the mīm and fatḥa on the fāʾ, which is a man who flees much, like Imruʾ al-Qays's saying describing his horse:

4411 - مِكَّرٍّ مِفَرٍّ مُقْبِلٍ مُدْبِرٍ معاً ... كجُلْمودِ صَخْرٍ حَطَّهُ السيلُ مِنْ عَلِ
(Gloss: Charging, retreating, advancing, withdrawing all at once, like a boulder of rock hurled down by the torrent from on high.)

Most use of this pattern is for instruments.

semin-durr:11-11.t:
His saying: {كَلاَّ لاَ وَزَرَ}: The discussion of «كلا» has been given earlier. The khabar of «لا» is omitted, that is, "there is no refuge for him." Is this clause reported as the speech of man, in which case it is accusative in position, or is it resumptive, a report from Allah the Exalted about that? «الوَزَرُ» is the refuge, whether a fortress, a mountain, or a weapon. He said:

4412 - لَعَمرُكَ ما للفتى مِنْ وَزَرْ ... من الموتِ يُدْرِكُه والكِبَرْ
(Gloss: By your life, a young man has no refuge from death, which overtakes him, nor from old age.)

semin-durr:12-12.t: His saying: {المستقر}: It is a mubtadaʾ, its khabar being the preposition-and-noun phrase before it. It may be a maṣdar in the sense of "settling", and it may be the place of settling. «ويومَئذٍ» is accusative by an implied verb, and it is not accusative by «مُسْتقر»: if it is a maṣdar, because it precedes it; and if it is a place, because it has no governing power at all.

semin-durr:14-14.t:
His saying: {بَصِيرَةٌ}: Several analyses are possible. The first: that it is a khabar of «الإِنسانُ», and «على نفسِه» is attached to «بَصيرةٌ». The meaning: "Rather, man is a witness against himself." On this, for what reason was the khabar made feminine? The grammarians differed about that. Some said the hāʾ in it is for intensification. Al-Akhfash said: "It is like your saying: so-and-so is an example (ʿibra) and a proof (ḥujja)." It is also said that what is meant by man is his limbs, as if He said: "Rather, his limbs are witnesses (baṣīra)," that is, attesting. The second: that it is a mubtadaʾ, and «على نفسِه» its khabar, the clause being the khabar of «الإِنسانُ». On this there are interpretations. One: that «بصيرةٌ» is an adjective of an omitted noun, that is, "a seeing eye." Al-Farrāʾ said it. And he recited:

4413 - كأن على ذي العقْل عَيْناً بَصيرةً ... بمَقْعَدِه أو مَنْظَرٍ هو ناظرُهْ
يُحاذِرُ حتى يَحْسَبَ الناسَ كلَّهمْ ... من الخوف لا تَخْفَى عليهمْ سرائِرُهْ
(Gloss: It is as if over the man of intellect there were a watching eye, over his seat or any sight he beholds. He is so wary that, out of fear, he thinks all people, that his secrets are not hidden from them.)

The second: that the meaning is "seeing limbs". The third: that the meaning is "seeing angels", and the tāʾ on this is for the feminine. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "«بصيرة» is a clear proof, described as 'seeing' by figurative usage, as the signs were described as seeing in His saying {فَلَمَّا جَآءَتْهُمْ آيَاتُنَا مُبْصِرَةً} [al-Naml: 13]." I say: This holds if you do not make «الحُجَّة» an expression for man, or make the entry of the tāʾ for intensification. But if it is for intensification, the attribution of seeing to it is literal. The third of the previous analyses: that the khabar is the preposition-and-noun phrase, with «بصيرةٌ» its agent; this is preferable to what precedes it, because the original in predication is the singular.

semin-durr:15-15.t:
His saying: {وَلَوْ ألقى}: This clause is circumstantial (ḥāl). A parallel has been given more than once. «المعاذير» is the plural of «مَعْذِرة» irregularly, like «مَلاقيح» and «مَذاكير», the plurals of «لَقْحَة» and «ذَكَر». The grammarians have two views on such a case. The first: that it is a plural of a word actually used, namely «لَقْحَة» and «ذَكَر». The second: that it is a plural of a word not used, but of an implied one, that is, «مَلْقَحَة» and «مِذْكار». Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: is the rule for «المَعْذِرَة» not to be pluralised as «معاذِرَ», not «معاذير»? I say: «المعاذير» is not a plural of «مَعْذِرة» but a collective noun (ism jamʿ) for it, like «المَناكير» for «المُنْكر»." The Shaykh said: "This pattern is not among the patterns of collective nouns, but among the patterns of broken plurals." End of quotation, and he is correct. It is also said: «معاذير» is the plural of «مِعْذار», which is a curtain, so the meaning is: "even if he let down his curtains." «المعاذِيْرُ» are curtains in the language of Yemen. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddī said it, and it was recited in support:

4414 - ولكنَّها ضَنَّتْ بمَنْزلِ ساعةٍ ... علينا وأَطَّتَ فوقَها بالمعَاذِرِ
(Gloss: But she was stingy with an hour's lodging for us, and creaked above it with the curtains.)

He dropped the yāʾ from «المعاذير» out of poetic necessity. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If it is correct, I mean that «المعاذير» are the curtains, it is because it prevents the seeing of the one concealed, as an excuse prevents the punishment of the sinner." I say: This statement of his may be an explanation of the common meaning between "curtains" and "excuses", and it may be an explanation of the relation permitting the figurative usage.

semin-durr:17-17.t:
His saying: {وَقُرْآنَهُ}: that is, its recitation; so it is a maṣdar annexed to its object. As for the agent, it is omitted. The original is: "and your reciting it." «القرآن» is a maṣdar in the sense of recitation. Ḥassān, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

4415 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... يُقَطِّعُ الليلَ تَسْبيحاً وقُرآناً
(Gloss: [first hemistich missing in the source] ... He spends the night in glorification and recitation.)

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Abū al-ʿĀliya said: «إنَّ علينا جَمْعَه وقُرانَه. فإذا قَرَتَه فاتَّبِعْ قُرانَه» with fatḥa on the qāf, the rāʾ and the tāʾ, without hamza or alif." I say: He did not mention an analysis. As for the analysis of «جَمْعَه وقُرانَه» and «فاتَّبِعْ قُرانَه», it is clear from what was said about Ibn Kathīr's reading in al-Baqara, and whether it is a transfer or from the root «قَرَن»; the verification of the two views is stated there, so consult it. As for his saying "with fatḥa on the qāf, the rāʾ and the tāʾ," meaning in «فإذا قَرَتَه», he points to its having been read anomalously in this way, and its analysis is that the original is «قَرَأْتَه», a past verb attributed to the second-person pronoun, that is, "when you wished to recite it"; then the hamza was turned into alif because of its quiescence after a fatḥa, then the alif was dropped for lightness, as in their saying «ولو تَرَ ما الصبيانَ», that is, «ولو تَرَى الصبيانَ», with «ما» redundant; so the word became «قَرَتَه», as you see.

semin-durr:20-20.t: His saying: {بَلْ تُحِبُّونَ}: Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read «يُحِبُّون» and «يَذَرون» with the yāʾ of the third person, following the wording «الإِنسان» mentioned first, because what is meant by it is the genus. The rest read both with the second person, either as an address to the disbelievers of Quraysh, or as a shift (iltifāt) away from reporting about the genus mentioned earlier and turning to it with address.

semin-durr:22-22.t:
His saying: {وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاضِرَةٌ}: There are several analyses. The first: that «وجوهٌ» is a mubtadaʾ, «ناضِرةٌ» its adjective, «يومَئذٍ» accusative by «ناضِرة», and «ناظرةٌ» its khabar, with «إلى ربِّها» attached to the khabar. The meaning: the radiant faces on the Day of Resurrection will be looking at Allah the Exalted. This is a sound meaning and an easy analysis. «الناضِرَةُ» is from «النُّضْرَةِ», which is living in comfort; from it comes «غُصْنٌ ناضِر» (a fresh branch). The second: that «وجوهٌ» is also a mubtadaʾ, with «ناضِرَةٌ» its khabar and «يومَئذٍ» accusative by the khabar, as above. What made the indefinite noun permissible as a mubtadaʾ here is that the place is one of enumeration (tafṣīl), as in his saying:

4416 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... فثوبٌ لَبِسْتُ وثوبٌ أَجُرّْ
(Gloss: [first hemistich missing in the source] ... one garment I wore, and another I trail.)

and «ناظرةٌ» would be an adjective of «وجوه», or a second khabar, or the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ; and «إلى ربِّها» is attached to «ناظرة» as above. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "He began with an indefinite because it was specified by His saying «يومئذٍ»." Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "The indefinite is permitted as mubtadaʾ here because of the attainment of benefit." I say: As for Ibn ʿAṭiyya's statement, there is something to consider in it, because his saying "it was specified by His saying «يومئذٍ»" means this specification is either because it governs it, which is impossible since it is a non-derived noun, or because it is described by it, which is also impossible, since bodies are not described by time, just as time is not predicated of them. As for Abū al-Baqāʾ's statement, if by the attainment of benefit he means the enumeration I put forward, it is correct; if he means what Ibn ʿAṭiyya meant, it is not correct, for the reason you know.

The third: that «وجوهٌ» is a mubtadaʾ and «يومئذٍ» its khabar. Abū al-Baqāʾ said it. This is a sheer error, in meaning and in the craft. As for the meaning, there is no benefit in predicating that of them. As for the craft, time is not predicated of bodies, and if something with that appearance occurs, it is interpreted, such as «الليلةَ الهلالُ» (tonight, the new moon). The fourth: that «وجوهٌ» is a mubtadaʾ and «ناضرةٌ» its khabar, and {إلى رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ} a clause in the position of a second khabar. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said it. There is something to consider in it, because no sentence is formed from the two, since the apparent sense is that «إلى» is attached to «ناظرة»; unless he means that «ناظرةٌ» is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "they are looking toward their Lord", and this clause is a second khabar. There is arbitrariness in it.

The fifth: that the khabar of «وجوه» is implied, that is, "faces on that day are there," with «ناضرةٌ» an adjective and likewise «ناظرةٌ». Abū al-Baqāʾ said it. It is remote because there is no need of it. I do not know what impelled them to this given the clarity of the first analysis and its freedom from these arbitrary readings. That «إلى» is a preposition and «ربِّها» is made genitive by it is what comes first to the mind.

Some of the Muʿtazila analysed it by making «إلى» a singular noun meaning "favour (nʿima)", annexed to «الرَّبّ», pluralised as «آلاء», as in {فَبِأَيِّ آلاء رَبِّكُمَا تُكَذِّبَانِ} [al-Raḥmān: 13]; it has already been mentioned that it has four dialectal forms. «ربِّها» is genitive by annexation, and «إلى» is an object put first, governed by «ناظرةٌ» in the sense of «مُنْتظرة» (awaiting). The implied form: "radiant faces awaiting the favour of their Lord." This is a flight from affirming seeing for Allah the Exalted, according to their doctrine.

Al-Zamakhsharī contrived for the Muʿtazilī doctrine by another route, from the side of the grammatical craft. After making the fronting in «إلى ربها» a signal of exclusivity, he said: "What is sound along with it is that it be from people's saying «أنا إلى فلانٍ ناظرٌ ما يَصْنَعُ بي», meaning expectation and hope. From it is the saying of the one who said:

4417 - وإذا نَظَرْتُ إليك مِنْ ملكٍ ... والبحرُ دونَك زِدْتَني نِعَما
(Gloss: When I look to you, O king, with the sea before you, you increase me in favours.)

And I heard a woman from al-Sarāt begging in Mecca at midday, when people close their doors and retire to their siesta places, saying: «عُيَيْنتي ناظِرَةٌ إلى اللَّهِ وإليكم» (my little eye is looking to Allah and to you). The meaning: they do not expect favour and honour except from their Lord." I say: This is like circling around the view of those who say that «ناظرة» is in the sense of «مُنْتظرة». However, Makkī rejected this view, saying: "The entry of «إلى» with «النظر» shows that it is looking with the eye, and it is not from waiting; if it were from waiting «إلى» would not enter with it. Do you not see that you do not say «انتظرتُ إلى زيد» but you say «نظرْتُ إلى زيد»? So «إلى» accompanies looking with the eye and does not accompany the looking of waiting. Whoever says that «ناظرة» means «مُنتظرة» has erred in meaning and in grammatical analysis, and has put the speech in the wrong place."

«النُّضْرَةُ» is the freshness of the skin and its beauty, which is from the effect of comfort. One says «نَضِر وَجْهُه فهو ناضِرٌ». Some said: It is conceded that it is from the looking of the eye, but that is with an omitted muḍāf, that is, "the reward of their Lord," and the like. Makkī said: "If this were allowed, it would be allowed to say «نَظَرْتُ إلى زيد», meaning «إلى عطاءِ زيدٍ». In this is a violation of the speech of the Arabs and a confusion of meanings." «نَضَره الله» and «نَضَّره», lightened and with shadda, mean He beautified him and gave him comfort. In the hadith: "May Allah make radiant (naḍḍara) a man who heard my saying, retained it, and conveyed it as he heard it," it is related both ways. Gold is called «نُضار» from that. It is also called «النَّضْرُ», and «أخضرُ ناضِرُ» is like «أسودُ حالكٌ», and «قَدَحٌ نُضارٌ» and «نُضارٍ», related with agreement of case (ittibāʿ) and with annexation.

The majority read «ناضِرَة» with alif. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read «نَضِرَة» without it, like «فَرِحَ» and «فَرِحٌ».
